Before anything else

Six words you need first

Every later slide uses these words. Click a card to read it in full.

Biopharmaceutics

"Bio" means life; "pharmaceutics" means making the medicine. It studies how the drug's own properties, its dosage form and its route affect how fast and how much of it gets absorbed.

  • It links the physicochemical properties of the drug (solubility, pKa, particle size) to the response seen after giving it.
  • It looks at three things together: the drug, the dosage form (tablet, syrup, injection) and the route.
  • Its main output is the rate and extent of systemic absorption.

Pharmacokinetics (PK)

"What the body does to the drug." The drug's travel story: Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism and Excretion (ADME).

  • The same dose given to the same person gives similar drug-level curves each time.
  • The same dose given to different people gives different curves, because bodies differ.
  • Adding Liberation at the start and Response at the end turns ADME into LADMER.

Pharmacodynamics (PD)

The opposite view: "what the drug does to the body." That is the effect, the R in LADMER.

  • PK decides how much drug reaches the site of action, and when.
  • PD decides what happens when it gets there, such as a receptor switching on or off.

Bioavailability (F)

The fraction of a dose that reaches the bloodstream unchanged, and how fast it gets there. IV gives F = 100%.

  • Absorbed dose = F × dose. Example: F = 70% and a 500 mg dose → 350 mg absorbed.
  • Digoxin tablets have F = 0.62, so 250 mcg × 0.62 = 155 mcg absorbed.
  • It is measured using the AUC (area under the drug-level curve).

Systemic circulation

The main blood loop that the heart pumps to the whole body. A drug "counts" as absorbed only once it gets here.

  • A drug swallowed but still in the gut is not yet absorbed.
  • From the gut, blood first goes to the liver through the portal vein, and only then to the heart. That detour causes the first-pass effect.

First-pass effect

Drug taken by mouth passes through the gut wall and liver first, which break part of it down before it reaches the bloodstream.

  • Also called presystemic metabolism.
  • Fully affected: oral. Partly affected: rectal.
  • Not affected: IV, sublingual, buccal, IM, SC, inhalation, transdermal.

A memory trick from the review center

LUNA gets in, HIPE gets out

A drug's chemistry decides where it goes. Fat-loving, uncharged drugs cross membranes and get absorbed. Water-loving, charged drugs stay in body fluids and get excreted.

How a drug moves from LUNA to HIPE

  • The liver adds polar groups (Phase I and II), which turns a LUNA drug into a HIPE metabolite, except acetylation and methylation, which make the drug less polar.
  • In the kidney, unionized drug is reabsorbed back into the blood, while ionized, polar drug stays in the urine and leaves.
  • Board trick: to clear a weak acid faster (e.g. aspirin overdose), make the urine alkaline so the acid stays ionized and trapped in urine.

Sources: MSD Manual, Drug Excretion; Philippine pharmacy review notes (LUNA/HIPE).

Routes · 2 of 4

Enteral: through the gut

"Enteral" means using the digestive tract, from the mouth to the rectum. Where along the tract the drug is absorbed decides how much the liver sees first.

Parenteral: injections outside vessels

"Parenteral" means bypassing the gut. These injections go into muscle or skin layers, and the drug then soaks into nearby capillaries. That still counts as an absorption step.

Topic 2 · Factors affecting absorption

The wall every drug must cross

The cell membrane is a lipid bilayer (fluid mosaic): water-loving heads face out, oily tails face in, with cholesterol and proteins mixed in. Below, real molecules try to cross it.

Outside the cell (extracellular fluid)Inside the cell (cytoplasm)Click the cell membrane to zoom in

Cross easily: small, oily, uncharged

  • O₂ and CO₂: tiny, non-polar gases that dissolve straight into the oily core.
  • Ethanol: small and only slightly polar, so it slips through.
  • Steroid-like lipophilic drugs: fat-loving ring structures that cross easily.
  • Unionized aspirin (in the stomach): the uncharged acid form crosses.

Blocked: large, polar, charged

  • Glucose: covered in polar –OH groups, so it needs a carrier protein.
  • Na⁺ ion: charged and wrapped in a water shell. Bare bilayers are about 10⁹ times less permeable to ions than to water.
  • Ionized aspirin (A⁻): the charged form bounces off.
  • Insulin: a protein (macromolecule), far too big. That is why it is injected, not swallowed.

Dosage form factors

LDFs absorb faster than SDFs. Click for release types.

SDFs · solid dosage forms

Tablets, capsules. Must first disintegrate, then dissolve, before absorption.

LDFs · liquid dosage forms

Solutions, suspensions, emulsions. No disintegration step; a solution is already dissolved.

LDFs have a FASTER rate of absorption than SDFs.

Usual speed of absorption
Solution›Suspension›Capsule›Tablet›Coated tablet›Extended release
Release types of solid dosage forms
  • Immediate release (IR): releases the whole dose promptly after swallowing. Fast peak, short effect.
  • Modified release (MR): umbrella term; the timing or place of release is changed on purpose. Covers delayed release (e.g. enteric-coated, opens in the intestine) and extended release.
  • Extended release (ER / XR): releases slowly over many hours, so it can be given at least half as often (e.g. once instead of twice a day).
  • Sustained release (SR): a type of extended release that keeps releasing drug over a long time, keeping blood levels up longer (not always perfectly steady; a steady rate is controlled release).

Three families of factors

Body · Drug · Formulation. Click for the list.

  • Body: membrane, gut pH, blood flow, surface area, gastric emptying, first-pass effect.
  • Drug: pH-partition, partition coefficient, dissolution, particle size, crystal form, polymorphism, stability, complexation.
  • Formulation: lubricants (more → slower dissolution), disintegrants (more → faster), coatings, and dosage form (solution > suspension > capsule > tablet > coated tablet).

Sources: Alberts, Molecular Biology of the Cell (NCBI NBK26815); OpenStax Biology, Components and Structure of the Membrane.

Topic 2 · Drug factors

Dissolve first, absorb later

This is the lab test pharmacists use: the USP paddle apparatus (37 °C, 900 mL, a rotating paddle). The tablet wets → disintegrates into granules → breaks into fine particles → dissolves. Only dissolved drug can be absorbed.

37 °C · 900 mL · paddle 50 rpmDots in the liquid = dissolved drug
Particle size: Form:
Stage
0%
of the dose dissolved

time 0 min

Noyes–Whitney equation

dCdt = D · A · (Cs − C)h

The next slide lets you change every letter.

Dissolution is the rate-limiting step for most oral solids.

Particle size, crystal form, polymorphs

↓ particle size → ↑ surface area → faster. Amorphous (less stable) dissolves faster than crystalline.

  • Polymorphism: the same drug packed in different crystal arrangements, which changes stability, solubility and dissolution.
  • Pseudopolymorphs (solvates): crystals that trap solvent; with water they are hydrates.

Stability · complexation · dosage form

Enteric coating (e.g. aspirin) passes the stomach intact. Tetracycline + Ca²⁺ → poor absorption. Griseofulvin ↑ with a fatty meal.

  • Enteric coating: an acid-resistant coat that stays intact in the stomach (pH 1–3) and dissolves in the small intestine (pH above about 5.5).
  • Aspirin: enteric-coated so the tablet passes the stomach intact and releases in the intestine, mainly to protect the stomach lining from irritation and bleeding.
  • Truly acid-unstable drugs (broken down by stomach acid): omeprazole, erythromycin, penicillin G. Coating or a different route keeps them from losing potency.
  • Fluoroquinolones or tetracyclines with dairy or antacids → decreased absorption.
  • Griseofulvin + fatty food: griseofulvin is a lipid-soluble (poorly water-soluble) drug. Taking it with a fatty meal increases absorption, because fat triggers bile release, and bile helps dissolve it.
  • A lipid-soluble drug + a water-soluble complexing agent (e.g. cyclodextrin) can increase absorption.
  • Liquid dosage forms are absorbed faster than solid ones.

Topic 2 · Body factors

How fast does the stomach empty?

Most drugs are absorbed in the intestine, not the stomach. So the faster the stomach empties, the sooner absorption starts. The rate is inversely proportional to the time spent in the stomach.

Gastric emptying simulator

Turn factors on and off.

Speeds up emptying
Slows emptying
1.0×
time the drug stays in the stomach

The multipliers are illustrative, not clinical values.

Blood flow

High blood flow → faster absorption. Blood carries absorbed drug away, keeping the gut-side level higher than the blood-side level.

The lungs receive all the blood the heart pumps, which is why inhaled drugs act so fast.

Food in the stomach

Fat slows emptying the most. Carbohydrates and amino acids slow it too.

Some drugs are labelled "take on an empty stomach" so they reach the intestine quickly. Others are taken with food to protect the stomach or to improve absorption of fat-soluble drugs.

Take on an empty stomach

Reach the intestine fast, or food blocks absorption: e.g. levothyroxine, alendronate, ampicillin.

Take with food

Protect the stomach (NSAIDs) or help fat-soluble drugs absorb (griseofulvin with a fatty meal).

Body position

Lying on the left side slows emptying, while lying on the right side helps, because the pylorus (the stomach's exit) points to the right.

Lying on the RIGHT side · ✗ acid flows up (more reflux) · ✓ faster emptyingLying on the LEFT side · ✓ acid stays in stomach (less reflux) · ✗ slower emptying

Topic 3

pH-partition theory

Many drugs are weak acids or weak bases, so part of each dose carries a charge (ionized) and part does not (unionized). Only the unionized form crosses the fat membrane. The pH of the place decides the split.

1 · Pick a drug

pKa3.5

2 · Pick a place

pH1.5
99%
unionized (can cross)
1%
ionized (blocked)

Stomach · pH 1.5Blood · pH 7.4Cyan = unionized · coral with ring = ionized

The rule

  • Weak acids are best absorbed at acidic pH.
  • Weak bases are best absorbed at basic pH.

An acid in an acidic place keeps its proton, so it stays uncharged. A base in a basic place does too.

Henderson–Hasselbalch

Acid: pH = pKa + log [A⁻] ionized[HA] unionizedBase: pOH = pKb + log [BH⁺] ionized[B] unionized

When pH = pKa, the drug is exactly 50% ionized. Every 1 pH unit away changes the ratio 10-fold.

The catch

Weak acids are still mostly absorbed in the small intestine.

The small intestine's huge surface area and high blood flow outweigh the less favorable pH. Vitamin C, for example, is absorbed in the small intestine.

Topic 5 · Pharmacokinetics

Pharmacokinetics and transport processes

Pharmacokinetics is "what the body does to the drug". Its four processes are I. Absorption, II. Distribution, III. Metabolism and IV. Excretion.

Fick's law of diffusion

Drug moves from high to low concentration; its speed depends on four things.

Rate of diffusion =CG × SA × DEMT
CG concentration gradient: the difference in drug level across the membrane
SA surface area of the membrane
DE diffusion coefficient: how easily the drug moves (small, lipid-soluble = high)
MT membrane thickness: thicker → slower

Topic 5 · Pharmacokinetics

Transport processes

Drugs cross cell membranes in six ways. Passive diffusion, governed by Fick's law (previous slide), is the most common.

Why profiles differ

  • Same dose of different formulations, same person → different concentration–time profiles.
  • Same dose of a drug, different people → different concentration–time profiles.

Six ways to cross the membrane

ProcessNeeds energy?DirectionCarrier protein?Saturable?Key points
  • Passive diffusion✗ NoDown (high → low)✗ No✗ NoMost common, but slowest.
  • Facilitated transport✗ NoDown (high → low)✓ Yes✓ YesCarrier-mediated, no energy needed.
  • Active transport✓ ATPAgainst (low → high)✓ limited✓ YesFastest; carriers are few, so it saturates.
  • Convective transport✗ NoWith water flow✗ No✗ NoPore / bulk flow between cells. Small water-soluble drugs; cations pass easier (pores are negative).
  • Vesicular transport✓ Yes—✗ No—Drug need not be dissolved. Pinocytosis (vit A, D, E, K), phagocytosis, endo-/exocytosis.
  • Ion-pair transport✗ NoDown (high → low)✗ No✗ NoFor highly ionized drugs: cation + anion → neutral pair that crosses.

Topic 6 · Bioavailability and bioequivalence

Bioavailability (F): how much gets in?

Not every milligram swallowed reaches the blood. Bioavailability is the ability of a drug to be absorbed and used by the body: the rate and extent at which it enters the systemic circulation and so reaches its site of action.

Three ways to say it

  • The ability of the drug to be absorbed and used by the body.
  • The rate and extent at which a drug enters the systemic circulation, thereby accessing the site of action.
  • The fraction (relative amount) of the dose that reaches the general circulation.
F =amount reaching the systemic circulationdose givenIV: F = 1 (100%)

Absorbed dose = F × dose

Topic 6 · Bioavailability and bioequivalence

Absolute vs relative bioavailability

Both compare AUCs, corrected for dose. They differ only in what the drug is compared against.

Absolute bioavailability

  • Compares a non-IV dose vs IV.
  • Standard: IV, because it has 100% F (no absorption step).
Fabs = AUCoral ÷ DoseoralAUCIV ÷ DoseIV

Relative bioavailability

  • Comparison of two non-IV dosage forms (or brands).
  • Example: oral solution vs oral tablet.
Frel = AUCtest ÷ DosetestAUCreference ÷ Dosereference
Sample problem 1

20 mg was given to three groups. AUCs: oral liquid 1340, oral capsule 1190, IV bolus 1620 mg·h/L. Find the absolute BA of the liquid and the capsule.

Topic 6 · Bioavailability and bioequivalence

Bioequivalence: same drug, same exposure?

Bioequivalence compares the bioavailabilities of different formulations, drug products or batches of the same drug product. It is established when two products have similar bioavailability.

Biopharmaceutics Classification System (BCS)

Sorts drugs by two things: how well they dissolve (solubility) and how well they cross the gut wall (permeability).

ClassSolubilityPermeabilityWhat limits absorptionExamples
  • Class I★ BiowaiverHighHighGastric emptying (absorbs easily)Metoprolol, propranolol, diltiazem, verapamil, paracetamol
  • Class IILowHighDissolution: improve it with smaller particles or a fatty mealGriseofulvin, ketoconazole, carbamazepine, phenytoin, nifedipine, ibuprofen
  • Class IIIHighLowPermeability: dissolves well but crosses the membrane poorlyAtenolol, metformin, cimetidine, ranitidine, acyclovir
  • Class IVLowLowBoth: poor and variable oral absorptionFurosemide, hydrochlorothiazide, paclitaxel
High solubility: the highest dose dissolves in ≤ 250 mL of water across pH 1–6.8.
High permeability: ≥ 85% of the dose is absorbed (older FDA rule: ≥ 90%).
★ Class I = biowaiver: its bioequivalence can be shown by a lab dissolution test instead of a human study. (Some Class III drugs also qualify.)

Measure three ratios

  • AUC ratio = AUCgeneric ÷ AUCreference (extent)
  • Cmax ratio = Cmax generic ÷ Cmax reference (rate)
  • Tmax ratio = Tmax generic ÷ Tmax reference
Similarity is established if each ratio falls within 80–125% at a 90% confidence interval.

Key terms related to BE

Generic, pharmaceutical and therapeutic substitution are on the next slide.

Why it matters

  • Bioequivalent products can be substituted for each other.
  • Too little exposure → the drug may fail. Too much or too fast → side effects.
  • The real test requires the whole 90% CI of each ratio to sit inside 80–125%.

Topic 7 · Distribution

Drug distribution: where does it go?

Distribution is the transfer of drug from the blood into the tissues after absorption: the drug leaves the systemic circulation and enters the extravascular (tissue) spaces.

Blood flow / perfusion

  • Cardiac output: volume of blood pumped by the heart in 1 minute (about 5 L/min at rest).
  • Perfusion: the flow of blood or fluid to tissues and organs, i.e. the fraction of cardiac output delivered to a specific tissue or organ.

Other factors affecting distribution

  • Lipophilicity: lipophilic (non-polar) drugs enter tissues more than hydrophilic (polar) ones.
  • Size: smaller molecules distribute more than larger ones.
  • pH: unionized drug crosses membranes; ionized drug is held back.
  • Protein binding: only free (unbound) drug leaves the blood. Bound drug is a reservoir.
  • Protein displacement: a second drug pushes the first off albumin, so free levels rise (e.g. warfarin displaced by aspirin or sulfonamides → bleeding risk).
Highly perfused organsDrag to turn · scroll to zoom

Special barriers

Blood–brain barrier
  • Requirement: lipophilic (lipid-soluble, unionized, small).
Placenta
  • Requirement: lipophilic, unionized and small; most such drugs reach the fetus.
Mammary gland
  • Requirement: lipophilic and unionized.
  • Milk is acidic (about pH 7.0, vs plasma 7.4).
  • Weak acids: ionize less in milk, so they stay in plasma.
  • Weak bases: ionize in milk and get trapped, so they concentrate in milk.

Topic 7 · Distribution

Volume of distribution (Vd) and loading dose

Vd is the volume the drug would need to fill to give the same concentration it currently has in the blood. It is not a real body space: a drug soaked up by tissues leaves little in plasma, so its Vd looks huge.

Trend and importance

  • High Vd: the drug is highly distributed into tissues.
  • Low Vd: the drug stays mostly in the blood (plasma).
  • ↑ Vd → ↑ half-life (t½ = 0.693 × Vd ÷ CL).
  • ↑ Vd → ↑ clearance (CL = k × Vd).

Loading dose (LD)

  • Usually given as a single dose to reach the desired plasma concentration quickly.

Topic 8 · Metabolism

Drug metabolism: making drugs easy to remove

Also known as biotransformation (formerly called detoxification). It converts drugs into water-soluble, less toxic and inactive metabolites. The major organ is the liver.

Exemptions

Prodrugs: inactive drug → active metabolite
  • Levodopa → dopamine
  • Dipivefrin → epinephrine
  • Enalapril → enalaprilat
  • Fosphenytoin → phenytoin
Toxic metabolites
  • Paracetamol → NAPQI (liver-toxic)

First-pass effect

  • Also known as first-pass metabolism or presystemic metabolism.
  • Drugs are metabolized after absorption but before reaching the systemic circulation.
  • Biggest for oral drugs; bypassed by IV, sublingual, transdermal and other non-oral routes.

Where an oral dose gets chipped away

The percentages are illustrative. Each stop removes some of the dose before it reaches the blood.
Phases of metabolism · click a phase
Some drugs go straight to phase II. After phase I a drug may be activated, unchanged, or (most often) inactivated.

Topic 8 · Metabolism · Phase I

Phase I: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis

Phase I adds or uncovers a polar group. Oxidation by the cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes is the most common route. Click a CYP row to focus on it.

*General inducers: anticonvulsants (barbiturates, phenytoin, carbamazepine), antibiotics (rifampicin), chronic alcohol, St. John's wort.
General inhibitors: anti-ulcer drugs (cimetidine, omeprazole), antimicrobials (chloramphenicol, macrolides, ritonavir, ketoconazole), acute alcohol.

CYP3A4 handles about 60% of the drugs in the PDR.

Other oxidizing enzymes

  • MAO-A metabolizes serotonin, norepinephrine (and dietary tyramine).
  • MAO-B metabolizes dopamine.
  • Dehydrogenases (e.g. alcohol dehydrogenase) metabolize ethanol and methanol.

Reduction

  • Reductases: nitro- and azo-reduction, e.g. chloramphenicol (nitro) and prontosil (azo).

Hydrolysis

  • Esterases (and amidases) split esters and amides.
  • Examples: ASA (aspirin) and ester anesthetics (e.g. procaine).

Topic 8 · Metabolism · Phase II

Phase II: conjugation

An enzyme attaches a large group (glucuronic acid, acetyl, glutathione, sulfate, methyl or an amino acid) to the drug. Most conjugates are water-soluble and leave in urine or bile. Pick a pathway to watch it happen.

Drugs and uses

    Acetylation · N-acetyltransferase (NAT2)

    Slow vs fast acetylators. Drugs: Hydralazine, Isoniazid, Procainamide, Dapsone. Click for more.

    • Slow acetylators: decreased or absent NAT activity → drug builds up → toxicity (e.g. isoniazid peripheral neuropathy; drug-induced lupus with hydralazine or procainamide).
    • Fast acetylators: increased NAT activity → drug cleared quickly → reduced effect (therapeutic failure).
    • Isoniazid: NAT2 makes acetylisoniazid; an amidase (induced by rifampicin) splits it to acetylhydrazine, which CYP2E1 (also induced by rifampicin) turns into toxic metabolites that harm the liver. The hydrazine pathway is favoured in slow acetylators.

    Remember

    • Glucuronidation is the most common phase II pathway.
    • Neonates have low UGT activity, so chloramphenicol builds up (gray baby syndrome).
    • Acetylation and methylation are exceptions: they make the drug slightly less water-soluble.

    Topic 8 · Metabolism · Drug interactions

    Enzyme induction vs inhibition

    Some drugs and foods change how many CYP enzymes the liver has, or block them. That changes how fast other drugs are cleared.

    Enzyme induction vs inhibition · warfarin example

    Pick what the patient also takes.

    Inducers · "PRCSG"

    Phenobarbital (barbiturates), phenytoin, primidone, rifampicin, carbamazepine, chronic alcohol, char-broiled food, St. John's wort, smoking, griseofulvin

    Inhibitors · "MEDVICKGA"

    Metronidazole, erythromycin, disulfiram, diltiazem, diphenhydramine, verapamil, isoniazid, chloramphenicol, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, grapefruit juice, acute alcohol

    Enzyme induction

    • ↑ enzyme = ↑ metabolism (↓ plasma concentration).
    • General result: ↓ drug activity.
    • Example: St. John's wort. Warfarin + St. John's wort → weaker warfarin, clot risk.

    Enzyme inhibition

    • ↓ enzyme = ↓ metabolism (↑ plasma concentration).
    • General result: ↑ drug activity or toxicity.
    • Example: grapefruit juice. Warfarin + grapefruit → bleeding risk.

    Special consideration: neonates

    • ↓ enzyme capacity.
    • ↓ clearance = ↑ t½.

    Topic 8 · Metabolism · Drug interactions

    Inducers and inhibitors: prodrug or not?

    Most drugs are already active, and metabolism switches them off. A prodrug is the opposite: it is inactive until an enzyme switches it on. So the same inducer or inhibitor can have opposite effects.

    Enzyme INDUCERS

    Example: rifampicin + oral contraceptive pill → the pill may fail.

    Example: grapefruit juice + felodipine → low blood pressure.

    Topic 9 · Excretion

    Drug excretion: the way out

    Excretion is the irreversible removal of drug from the body. To be excreted by the kidney, a drug should be water-soluble (polar), ionized and not bound to protein.

    Process of renal excretion · click a step

    Urine pH6.0

    Glomerular filtration · Cockcroft–Gault

    CrCl = (140 − age) × weight (kg)72 × SCr (mg/dL) × 0.85 if female
    AgekgSCr
    78
    mL/min

    Minor routes of excretion

    • Pulmonary excretion: volatile substances and gases (nitrous oxide, ethanol).
    • Biliary excretion: drug goes into bile → small intestine. Biliary recycling (enterohepatic circulation): the drug is reabsorbed back into the blood. Requirement: large (MW above about 500), polar, often conjugated.

    Mammary excretion

    • Milk is more acidic than plasma.
    • Weak acids will stay in plasma (less goes into milk).
    • Weak bases will be trapped in milk (ion trapping).
    • So weak bases concentrate more in breast milk.

    Topic 9 · Reaction kinetics

    Zero order vs first order

    In first order, a constant fraction is lost per unit time, so the rate depends on concentration. In zero order, a constant amount is lost per unit time, no matter the concentration.

    0

    Zero order

    A constant amount is lost per unit time. The rate does not depend on how much drug is left.

    Rate− dCdt = k0
    LineC = C0 − k0t
    Half-lifet½ = 0.5 C0k0
    Shelf lifet90 = 0.1 C0k0
    C vs time: straight
    ln C vs time: curved
    Rate vs C: flat
    k unitconc ÷ time (mg/mL/day)
    Examplesethanol; phenytoin and aspirin at high doses
    Half-lifegets shorter as C falls
    1

    First order

    A constant fraction (percent) is lost per unit time. The rate rises with concentration.

    Rate− dCdt = kC
    Lineln C = ln C0 − kt
    Half-lifet½ = 0.693k
    Shelf lifet90 = 0.105k
    C vs time: curved
    ln C vs time: straight
    Rate vs C: rising
    k unittime⁻¹ (e.g. day⁻¹)
    Examplesmost drugs
    Half-lifeconstant
